messages.content:
You are an evidence extraction specialist for PFAS treatment and remediation
research. Build a structured study evidence table before any narrative review
is written.

Extract one record per primary-study experiment, modeled scenario, or field
deployment that contributes usable evidence to the review task. A paper may
produce more than one record only when materially different matrices,
technologies, operating regimes, or endpoints would otherwise be conflated.

Review articles and perspectives may help identify terminology or primary
studies, but they must not be used as the source of a quantitative study
record. Never copy a review table as though it were a primary result.

For every populated source-dependent field:
- preserve the PFAS identity or class, matrix, starting concentration or
  loading, operating conditions, study scale, measured endpoint, value, unit,
  and material qualifiers when reported;
- attach only the field-level evidence locator identifiers that directly
  support that specific value or statement;
- use an empty string or empty array when the source does not report the
  information; do not infer or estimate it;
- do not turn the absence of information in the supplied packet into a study
  finding, quantitative result, or author-reported limitation unless the source
  explicitly states that absence;
- distinguish removal, separation, sorption, parent-compound loss,
  transformation, degradation, destruction, defluorination, mineralization,
  total organofluorine change, and toxicity change;
- classify endpoint_type from what was actually measured, not from the
  authors' preferred label. Parent loss alone is not destruction. Phase
  transfer is removal or separation, not degradation. Inorganic fluoride
  release or fluorine-balance closure can establish defluorination but cannot
  by itself establish mineralization. Use mineralization only when direct
  carbon-fate evidence such as CO2/inorganic-carbon production or a carbon
  balance is reported. Preserve a broader author term in reported_term and
  explain any mismatch in interpretation;
- do not normalize or compare values unless their units, denominators,
  matrices, PFAS scope, operating conditions, and endpoints permit it.

Only populate quantitative_findings when the source reports an actual numeric
value, inequality, approximate value, range, or explicit ND/not-detected
result. Put the number or censoring marker in value and the measurement unit in
unit. Normalize Unicode inequality signs to ASCII >= or <= and range dashes to
an ASCII hyphen while preserving the source wording in qualifiers. A unit or
order-of-magnitude scale without a number is not a quantitative finding.
Qualitative parent loss, intermediate formation, or disappearance belongs in
the endpoint interpretation or residual/byproduct statements instead.

Set value_form to exactly one of:
- exact_numeric: a bare number such as `99.7` or `1.2e-3`;
- approximate_numeric: `~` followed by a number;
- inequality: `<`, `<=`, `>`, or `>=` followed by a number;
- range: two numbers separated by `-` or `to`; or
- not_detected: exactly `ND`, `N/D`, `not detected`,
  `below detection limit`, or `below quantification limit`.

Put uncertainty, denominators, fold-change wording, and explanatory text in
qualifiers rather than value. A deterministic validator will remove malformed
quantitative fields before source verification.

For limitations, use basis=author_reported only when the source states the
limitation. Use basis=design_inferred only for a constraint that follows
directly from cited design evidence, such as one matrix, one compound, or
bench-scale operation. Never label missing information in the supplied packet
as a scientific limitation of the study.

Mark each record as comparable with conditions, descriptive only, or not
comparable. Comparability is an analyst inference rather than a quotation:
attach locators for the matrix, scale, conditions, endpoint, and denominator
on which the inference rests, and explain the reason. Do not reward a study
for reporting a larger percentage when its endpoint or conditions differ.

The task was derived from a defining review that is held out from all
candidate retrieval systems. The supplied anchor identifiers are an exclusion
list, not evidence. Do not extract from the anchor, cite it, reconstruct its
conclusions, or use its tables.

Return one JSON object that follows the supplied evidence-table schema exactly.
Do not write the narrative review in this step.

records.citation: McCleaf, P.; Englund, S.; Östlund, A.; Lindegren, K.; Wiberg, K.; Ahrens, L. Removal efficiency of multiple poly- and perfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) in drinking water using granular activated carbon (GAC) and anion exchange (AE) column tests. Water Research 2017, 120, 77–87.

comparability.reason: Bench-scale AE column operated in continuous flow with defined EBCT, bed volume, PFAS-spiked finished drinking water, and a consistent breakthrough definition (C/C0 = 0.1), producing removal vs. bed volume data that are structurally comparable to other fixed-bed adsorption systems when adjusted for EBCT and influent concentrations.

endpoints.interpretation: PFAS removal assessed from effluent concentrations over time; breakthrough defined at C/C0 = 0.1 and expressed as bed volumes treated and time to breakthrough; model-derived half-saturation time (t) also used to characterize capacity and kinetics
endpoints.reported_term: removal efficiency and breakthrough bed volumes

endpoints.interpretation: Model parameter t used to describe time to half saturation of AE column for co-removal of 14 PFASs; longer t in Phase 2 interpreted as increased effective capacity potentially due to PFAS agglomeration on DOC-loaded media
endpoints.reported_term: half-saturation time (t) from Lin and Huang column model

limitations.statement: Column behavior exhibited two phases, with Phase 2 showing greater apparent removal capacity, likely related to PFAS agglomeration on DOC-loaded media; authors note that Phase 2 parameters may be more relevant for predicting DWTP performance.

The Lin and Huang model fit AE results better than GAC results (R2 = 0.92) but still showed compound-specific deviations, particularly for PFOA, indicating uncertainty in predictive capacity across PFAS.

Adsorption mechanisms and the role of PFAS aggregation on AE surfaces could not be conclusively determined; authors call for further surface-structure analyses (e.g., SEM) to verify agglomeration or micelle/hemi-micelle formation.
Bench-scale columns used one finished drinking water source and a fixed influent PFAS concentration, so scale-up to variable full-scale conditions and other source waters may be uncertain.

records.citation: McCleaf, P.; Englund, S.; Östlund, A.; Lindegren, K.; Wiberg, K.; Ahrens, L. Removal efficiency of multiple poly- and perfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) in drinking water using granular activated carbon (GAC) and anion exchange (AE) column tests. Water Research 2017, 120, 77–87.

comparability.reason: Bench-scale GAC column operated in continuous flow with defined EBCT, bed volume, PFAS-spiked finished drinking water, and common breakthrough definition (C/C0 = 0.1), enabling comparison with other fixed-bed adsorption studies provided differences in EBCT, influent quality, and PFAS mixture are considered.

endpoints.interpretation: PFAS removal assessed from effluent concentrations over time; breakthrough defined at C/C0 = 0.1 and expressed as bed volumes treated; attention to variation in breakthrough BVs by PFAS chain length and functional group.
endpoints.reported_term: removal efficiency and breakthrough bed volumes

limitations.statement: Removal efficiencies in the GAC column decreased from startup to final sampling for all PFASs except PFTeDA and PFDoDA, indicating limited capacity and complex loading effects that challenge simple extrapolation of early-time performance to media lifetime.
Breakthrough bed volumes and removal behavior varied substantially by PFAS chain length and functional group, so a single design safety factor cannot uniformly predict breakthrough for all PFASs.

Bench-scale GAC column used one PFAS mixture and one drinking water source; real full-scale systems may experience different competitive adsorption from varying DOC and co-contaminants, limiting direct scale-up.

operating_conditions.qualifiers: Approximately weekly collection of 1000 mL effluent samples for PFAS and 200 mL for TOC

operating_conditions.name: Backwashing
operating_conditions.qualifiers: Columns backwashed 2-6 min using reservoir water after each sampling to fluidize and remix media, mimicking full-scale filters

pfas_scope.value: Mixture of 14 PFASs at ~100 ng/L each (individual compounds not listed in supplied excerpts)

quantitative_findings.name: Final sampling bed volumes treated
quantitative_findings.qualifiers: Final sampling point for GAC column operation

quantitative_findings.name: Breakthrough criterion
quantitative_findings.qualifiers: Breakthrough bed volume defined at 10% of influent concentration at column outlet

quantitative_findings.name: Bed volumes at which PFDoDA and PFTeDA removal increased
quantitative_findings.qualifiers: Removal efficiencies for PFTeDA (C13) and PFDoDA (C11) increased after ~30,000 BV (described as total PFAS sorption of 25 mg/g dw resin) despite general declining removal for other PFASs.

quantitative_findings.name: Total PFAS sorption at ~30,000 BV
quantitative_findings.qualifiers: Total PFAS mass adsorbed on GAC at the point where increased removal efficiency of PFTeDA and PFDoDA observed; used as indicator of media loading.

study_scale.value: Bench-scale continuous-flow column test using granular activated carbon (GAC) with PFAS-spiked drinking water from a full-scale DWTP

treatment.value: Fixed-bed column packed with granular activated carbon operated in continuous flow with periodic backwashing
